analysis.one_liner: Uses a seniors' cost-of-living index for Social Security and lifts the payroll tax cap on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in April 2019, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment track the prices seniors actually pay, by having the Bureau of Labor Statistics publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers and using it for benefit increases. It would also phase out, and after 2025 eliminate, the cap on wages subject to Social Security taxes, so earnings above the cap are taxed like everything below it. A portion of those new taxes on high earners would be credited back to them as somewhat higher benefits, but most of the money would go toward the program's finances.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security retirees and disabled beneficiaries, who would get cost-of-living adjustments keyed to elderly spending patterns, which historically rise faster than the index now used, mainly because of health care costs. The program's trust fund also gains decades of added revenue from taxing earnings above the cap, strengthening benefits for future retirees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security retirees and disabled beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers tracking spending by people 62 and older, and requires Social Security to use it for the annual cost-of-living adjustment instead of the index for urban wage earners.

It phases out the cap on compensation subject to Social Security taxation over 2020-2025 and eliminates it after 2025; the cap was $132,900 in 2019. The change applies to both wage earners and the self-employed.

Earnings above the old cap would be included in the benefit formula only at low rates (3 percent and 0.25 percent factors), so high earners who pay the new taxes receive only a modest benefit credit while most of the revenue supports the program.

Any benefit increases from the new cost-of-living index would not count as income or resources for SSI or Medicaid eligibility, so low-income beneficiaries would not lose other aid because of the higher payment.

analysis.who_pays: High earners. Anyone making wages or self-employment income above the annual cap would pay the 12.4 percent combined Social Security tax on all of it after 2025, and self-employed high earners pay both the employee and employer shares. They would receive only a small increase in their own future benefits in return.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning above the payroll tax cap

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the cap would raise the combined 12.4 percent Social Security tax on high earners' full income, and self-employed professionals and business owners bear both halves of the tax on earnings above the cap.

Because above-cap earnings are credited to benefits only at low rates, the bill breaks the traditional link between what a worker pays into Social Security and what that worker gets back, which critics of this approach argue turns the program from earned insurance into redistribution and can weaken political support for it.

The new cost-of-living index would raise annual benefit increases for all beneficiaries, adding to program outlays at the same time the payroll changes add revenue; the two changes pull the trust fund in opposite directions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary working people the trade is favorable: better inflation protection for current and future beneficiaries, financed by a tax increase concentrated on the highest earners, with protection so the higher payments do not cost low-income seniors their SSI or Medicaid. The main honest objection is the tax burden on high-earning self-employed people and the weakened contribution-benefit link, which is a real design change but one whose cost falls on the top slice of earners.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote there, and expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on April 10, 2019, joined by three Democratic cosponsors.
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 116th Congress, and it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the payroll tax cap are better off because the bill died, since they would have paid Social Security tax on all their income after 2025. Opponents of expanding Social Security benefits also avoided the added outlays from the seniors' cost-of-living index.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and opponents of expanding benefits

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; it sat without action from April 2019 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call showing where the parties stood.

industries.note: After 2025 they would pay the 12.4 percent Social Security tax on all earnings rather than only the first roughly $133,000, receiving only a small benefit credit in return. The bill's added revenue for the program comes almost entirely out of this group's income.

The bill applies the same phase-out of the cap to self-employment income, and the self-employed pay both the employee and employer halves of the tax, a full 12.4 percent, on earnings above the old cap.
